lesson.topicTitle: The nature and variety of living organisms

specAnchors.text: describe the common features shown by eukaryotic organisms: plants, animals, fungi and protoctists Plants: these are multicellular organisms; their cells contain chloroplasts and are able to carry out photosynthesis; their cells have cellulose cell walls; they store carbohydrates as starch or sucrose. Examples include flowering plants, such as a cereal (for example, maize), and a herbaceous legume (for example, peas or beans). Animals: these are multicellular organisms; their cells do not contain chloroplasts and are not able to carry out photosynthesis; they have no cell walls; they usually have nervous co-ordination and are able to move from one place to another; they often store carbohydrate as glycogen. Examples include mammals (for example, humans) and insects (for example, housefly and mosquito). Fungi: these are organisms that are not able to carry out photosynthesis; their body is usually organised into a mycelium made from thread-like structures called hyphae, which contain many nuclei; some examples are single-celled; their cells have walls made of chitin; they feed by extracellular secretion of digestive enzymes onto food material and absorption of the organic products; this is known as saprotrophic nutrition; they may store carbohydrate as glycogen. Examples include Mucor , which has the typical fungal hyphal structure, and yeast, which is single-celled. Protoctists: these are microscopic single-celled organisms. Some, like Amoeba , that live in pond water, have features like an animal cell, while others, like Chlorella , have chloroplasts and are more like plants. A pathogenic example is Plasmodium , responsible for causing malaria.

primer.text: Eukaryotes are the organisms whose cells keep their DNA inside a nucleus surrounded by its own membrane. This note tours the four groups you must know — animals, plants, fungi and protoctists — and pins down the features that examiners expect you to list for each one, plus the drawings you should be able to interpret.

modules.title: The eukaryotic cell plan: one shared blueprint
sourceHeadings: Common Features of Eukaryotic Organisms: Basics
modules.opening: Every organism whose cells store DNA inside a membrane-bound nucleus counts as a eukaryote. That single design feature splits the living world into two camps, because prokaryotes keep their genetic material loose in the cytoplasm. Some eukaryotes build bodies made of many cells, while others live as a single cell, yet both forms belong here.
keyPoints: A eukaryotic cell keeps its chromosome inside a nucleus that has its own surrounding membrane.
The four eukaryote groups named in this course are animals, plants, fungi and protoctists.
Being eukaryotic does not fix body size: members can be built from many cells or just one.
Under a light microscope the shared nucleus with its surrounding membrane marks both animal and plant cells as eukaryotic.

low.restatement: Eukaryotes are the organisms whose cells have a nucleus enclosed by a membrane; the four groups to remember are animals, plants, fungi and protoctists.
low.analogy: Picture the nucleus as a locked office holding all the paperwork, while prokaryotes leave theirs on an open desk in the middle of the room.
low.examPointer: If a question hands you a micrograph, find the dark round shape ringed by a double line — that visible enclosed nucleus is your evidence for calling the cell eukaryotic.

medium.restatement: The membrane around the nucleus separates transcription from translation and is the universal eukaryotic signature; body design (one cell or many) is a separate, independent variable.
medium.analogy: Two houses can look completely different outside yet share identical wiring behind the walls — body plan varies, the enclosed-nucleus wiring never does.
medium.examPointer: Comparisons between eukaryotes and prokaryotes earn marks only if the nucleus (or its absence) is stated explicitly, so lead with it before any other feature.

modules.title: Animals, plants, fungi and protoctists: the four feature lists
modules.opening: Animals and plants are the two many-celled groups most people picture first, and their feature lists overlap more than students expect. Both are built from cells with enclosed nuclei, yet each carries a small set of traits the other lacks. Learning the pairs of contrasts — walls, chloroplasts, carbohydrate stores and feeding — earns the marks.
keyPoints: Animal cells have a surrounding membrane, an enclosed nucleus, mitochondria and no cell wall.
Animal bodies are many-celled and their carbohydrate store is glycogen.
Plant cells add a cell wall built with cellulose and chloroplasts that harvest light for photosynthesis.
Plant bodies are many-celled and their carbohydrate store is starch.

low.restatement: Animals: many cells, nucleus with its own membrane, no cell wall, glycogen as the store. Plants: the same core plan plus cellulose walls and chloroplasts, storing starch.
low.analogy: Think of two flats with identical heating (mitochondria) but only one installed with solar panels (chloroplasts) and reinforced outer walls (cellulose).
low.examPointer: Two-mark versions of this question usually want one animal-only feature and one plant-only feature — a wall with cellulose, chloroplasts, or starch versus the glycogen store.

medium.restatement: The contrasts that separate the two groups are structural (wall, chloroplast) and biochemical (starch versus glycogen storage), while nucleus, membrane and mitochondria stay common.
medium.analogy: Two factories may run the same power supply yet stock different warehouses: plants bank starch behind cellulose walls, animals bank glycogen in unwalled units.
medium.examPointer: When a question shows an unlabelled cell diagram, walls and chloroplasts identify plant cells; their absence with mitochondria visible points to animal material.

modules.title: Fungi and protoctists: the often-confused pair
modules.opening: Fungi and protoctists are the two groups candidates mix up most often. Fungi build bodies of thread-like hyphae, may be single-celled like yeast, and absorb food from their surroundings. Protoctists are the leftovers drawer of the classification: a very varied set of mostly single-celled organisms that fit none of the other three lists.
keyPoints: Multicellular fungi are built from hyphae, which are thread-like filaments carrying many nuclei.
Some fungi are single-celled, and yeast is the named example.
Protoctists form a very varied set whose members share no single defining trait beyond being eukaryotic.
Drawing and labelling fungal and protoctist cells is an explicitly named exam skill.

low.restatement: Fungi: hyphae threads, sometimes single cells such as yeast. Protoctists: a varied catch-all group of mostly microscopic eukaryotes.
low.analogy: If the classification were a block of flats, fungi would be the identical floor plan repeated along corridors, protoctists the odds-and-ends storage rooms.
low.examPointer: Practise sketching a labelled fungal cell and two contrasting protoctist cells — the note flags exactly this drawing skill.

medium.restatement: Fungal bodies are hyphal networks whose walls carry no cellulose and no chloroplasts ever appear; protoctist diversity means identification relies on ruling out the other groups' defining features.
medium.analogy: Fungi are a standardised building system; protoctists are a lost-property office — you identify an item by failing to match it to any other department.
medium.examPointer: If asked to justify a protoctist assignment, argue from elimination: not an animal, not a plant, not a fungus.

glossary.definition: An organism whose cells keep their DNA inside a nucleus enclosed by its own membrane.
One of the thread-like filaments, packed with nuclei, that builds the body of a multicellular fungus.
A varied eukaryotic organism that fits none of the animal, plant or fungal feature lists.
The plant organelle that harvests light energy to drive photosynthesis.
